title: The plunging price of thought
short: How fast the cost of a fixed AI benchmark score falls, 2023 to 2026
author: Luke Emberson, David Roodman (Epoch AI)
more_note: Published under CC BY 4.0. Its interactive overlay (3-D fits, heat maps, record timelines) is worth opening there; this page recomputes the model-free rate from the authors' released runs, tests it, and lets you explore every record staircase.
takeaway: On five benchmarks (AIME, FrontierMath tiers 1-3, GPQA Diamond, chess and a secret game's puzzles), from 2023 to mid-2026, the cheapest per-question cost of reaching a fixed score (tokens used times archived list prices, lower budgets simulated by truncating runs) fell about 47% a quarter, 13x a year, averaged over a lattice of dates and scores; 43% to 53% by benchmark, with no uncertainty reported by design.
verdict: Believe the order of magnitude: our port of the authors' code reproduces every model-free rate, and the pooled rate stays between 43% and 56% a quarter (9x to 25x a year) under every correction and averaging choice tried here. Read the exact 47% and the technology multiples as one averaging choice among several, the article's dated examples as partly wrong (o3 is dated to o3-mini's release), and "fastest right after SOTA" as true on three of five benchmarks.

Toby Ord's challenge and David Roodman's replies, on X

responses.t: Has anything got 100,000x cheaper? The headline merges capability and cost
responses.by: Toby Ord, with David Roodman's replies, on X
responses.n: Ord called the comparison chart and headline "incorrect": the method folds rising capability into one cost number, and the AI line in the chart does not flatten as a slowing rate should. Roodman: read 47% like inflation in chained dollars; the slowdown is in time since a level was SOTA, not since GPT-3; comparing technologies is "fraught". The same day the authors added the Limitations caveat that credits Ord. Ord then called the 725x GPQA drop "solid (though not necessarily representative)" and asked for more early examples.

responses.t: Price is not cost: subsidies and operating losses
responses.by: Replies to the launch thread and to Epoch's newsletter version (Jeffrey Lee Funk, Nils H. Lehr and others)
responses.n: List prices can sit below cost while labs lose money and hyperscalers subsidise; adding the losses back would flatten the curve. Another commenter: production work adds retries, checks and review, so the cost of a checked task falls more slowly. No author reply found.

responses.t: The price of intelligence is falling
responses.n: Quotes the 47% and adds his own reading: if frontier models get cheap to run this fast, open models are less of a threat to the labs than they look.

responses.t: A quality-adjusted price index for AI services (v2)
responses.n: A hedonic index over models on sale falls about 0.51 a year in log price, "entirely through the rising capability" of the models; its per-task data cover only 14 of the 87 cost-frontier models in this article's released data, so it says it cannot test the article's rate (and its v2 withdraws its own per-task result).

since.n: Two commits after the launch (a spreadsheet of technology declines on 22 September, a plot colour change on 24 September); none changes the analysis; no issues or pull requests (read 27 November 2026).

Gradient Updates (David Roodman, Lynette Bye) restates the findings without the chained-index caveat; the Epoch Brief of 8 October summarises it in a paragraph. No later Epoch analysis of prices found by 27 November.
